The Smart Ring Goes to Church

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk.
  • Sources indicate that the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps.
  • According to recent reports, both are first, in their own ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.

Sources indicate that the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.

According to recent reports, both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring debuted in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech manufacturer ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.

Another major player in prayer apps is Hallow, aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.

Head-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.

Recent findings suggest that for now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.

One addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa says he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.).

Both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia indicates he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”.

According to recent reports, both Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.

Xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he notes, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.

“A lot of our users not only ask questions about the Bible but also ask about themselves, their relationships with their wives, they’re being bullied at school," Xia says, stressing safeguards around data storage, encryption, and privacy. "Everyone is going to have some AI that they trust, and how they view that is built on their personal stuff, their private vulnerabilities.”.

According to recent reports, costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.

“The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa says. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”.

Recent findings suggest that smart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M, refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”.

Oura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.

Smart ring users flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell says. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.

AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a fresh phase for smart rings, states Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight. These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura, Ultrahuman, and Samsung.

The pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord, are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.

Campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she claims. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”.

Xia points to the Blessed app’s communities, including its Healing Room broadcast feature, which lets pastors go live with sermons. It's not in the Elah app yet, but it's on the roadmap. Costa says communal practice is a core pillar, highlighting the “social layer” of public notes made on Christian texts in-app and an upcoming Glorify Ring feature which will allow a user to pair their device with a family member’s ring: “When your loved one is feeling down, you’ll get a buzz to check in with them.”.

Own Your Intelligence: A How-To Guide

📅 19 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.

Recently, Alex Karp encouraged enterprises to âown the means of production.â Not long after, Satya Nadella declared that buying intelligence from a frontier lab is like paying twice: once with money, and once with the proprietary knowledge you reveal to make that intelligence useful.

The question everyone is asking: who should own the intelligence at the core of your business?

To be clear, owning your intelligence is not a mandate nor a recommendation to get off the labs. For many workloads, frontier APIs and agents are still the right answer. But across our portfolio, we are seeing more companies building their own AI capabilities for parts of their products, vertically integrating toward owning and shaping their weights.

A few weeks ago, Sequoia brought together a group of AI founders and builders for an event on owning your AI stack. We had Harvey give us the customer-back view. Then Mercor, Langchain, Trajectory, and Fireworks walked us through the technical building blocks in the post-training stack.

Across the talks, a clear playbook emerged.

First, the open-weight frontier has moved faster than anticipated. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are extremely good! Training on open models used to be a treadmillâ¦ you mightâve spent months fine-tuning, and the next frontier release would erase your gains. Now, you can start from a baseline close to the frontier.

In a recent development, second, the independent post-training stack has matured. Thanks to companies like Mercor and Fireworks, every tech giant can access the technology stack of a frontier research lab, from training to inference to human or synthetic data. With strong evals, harness engineering, post-training, and online learning, open models can now beat frontier models in specific domains.

According to recent reports, A year ago, you chose open weights when performance was something you could sacrifice. Now, it is becoming an existential and strategic question. The newest battleground is for the intelligence layer. Not your weights, not your product.

Thereâs no one-size-fits-all approach. In addition to performance, there may be slices of your product where renting intelligence becomes a constraint because ofâ¦.

1. Cost. The more successful your AI product, the higher your AI COGS. If inference costs scale directly with usage, owning the model is the best way to protect your margins.

2. Speed. If youâre operating in a domain like coding (tab autocomplete) or cybersecurity, a small distilled custom model might beat a large general one, because speed is so important.

Sources indicate that 3. Proprietary data. If your feedback, evals, customer interactions, or domain data are what make the system better, you might prefer that data stays within your walls.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Controlling your destiny. The app layer and the intelligence layer are starting to merge. The labs are moving up into product, and app companies are moving down into the training loops that define how the product thinks. Owning the product increasingly might mean controlling more of the learning loop and the intelligence itself (h/t Harvey Research, RampLabs, Glean, Factory, and more).

In a recent development, assuming you've decided on your strategy for what to own vs. rent, the question becomes: how do you go from zero to one?

In a recent development, build your team. Don't shoehorn this into a platform team. Owning your intelligence needs people playing offense: building evals, shaping data, experimenting with open models, tuning harnesses, and pushing performance in a domain. Small, de novo teams go very far here, partnering with half a dozen ecosystem partners. Harvey, for example, has done a surprising amount of research with a team of just seven people!

Recent findings suggest that make the work legible. Every buyer right now is choosing their AI champion. Increasingly, the tiebreaker is published research, benchmarks, or technical posts. If you choose to do wonderful research in-house, share it with the ecosystem.

It has been revealed that execute the technical steps. Weâve laid out a high level framework below.

Harveyâs Gabe Pereyra stated it well: "If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models.â.

An eval is a set of tasks that measures whether your system can do the work well. Every task contains a prompt, context the model can use, and a grader. Most evals start as a founder squinting at outputs and vibe-checking whether they feel right. The goal is to turn that judgement into something repeatable.

In a recent development, harvey built its Legal Agent Benchmark by turning real legal work into discrete tasks a model could be tested on. The first iteration includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

In a recent development, itâs vital to have an eval before making the decision to own your intelligence. Once every forward pass has an eval, deciding which model to use can be a measured decision instead of a guess.

2/ Harness and context engineering.

It has been revealed that an agent has three parts: the model, the context, and the harness. The harness governs the product logic around the model: routing, retrieval, tools, memory, fallbacks, and traces. Harrison Chaseâs simple framing was that "the main job of the harness is to bring context to the model at the right point in time." The more out of distribution the task is for the model, the worse the off-the-shelf harness will be.

Industry observers note that A good harness lets you route tasks to the best model for your specific job, reuse the same evals across models, and decide what context and tools an agent gets. It also makes the agent inspectable. You can trace what context went in, which tools were called, and where it got stuck.

Post-training covers several techniques. The right one depends on what youâre trying to improve.

Industry observers note that lin Qiao laid it out: if the model is missing facts, you don't need to post-train - just use context or RAG. If the output format or behavior is wrong, use supervised fine-tuning. If the issue is product taste, use preference tuning. If the model needs to improve at a specialized task, use RL. If the model is too slow or expensive, distill it.

The goal is to pick the lightest method that moves your eval. Then serve the model through the same harness and measure quality, latency, and cost as it runs.

Once the system has its pieces â evals, harness, and model â the final step is improving that system in production.

Recent findings suggest that arjun Karanam made a good point: models keep getting smarter, but every session feels like it's their first day on the job. You can put Terence Tao in an accounting firm, but chances are (at least on day 1) he wonât be the best accountant there. What's missing is experience, not intelligence. Agents create that experience as they run.

Industry observers note that A trajectory is the path through the task: the context the model saw, the tools and sub-agents it called, the answer it produced, and what the user edited, undid, or retried. Capturing those trajectories in a tool like LangChain's LangSmith is necessary to build a continuous production loop. A failed task becomes an eval. Missing information goes into context or memory. A bad tool response becomes a harness fix.

Buyer beware: owning your intelligence opens Pandoraâs box.

Recent findings suggest that the closed-model stack is simple. You call a frontier model, use an out-of-the-box harness (e.g., Claude Code or Codex), add prompts and context, and ship. That gives you a high floor, but also a lower ceiling.

In a recent development, owning your stack means taking on more of the system yourself. The production stack becomes your open-source model, custom harness, tools, and context. The development stack becomes your proprietary evals, domain data, and online learning loop.

It is certainly more work! It potentially gives you a lower floor â but it also raises the ceiling.

Industry observers note that the labs will keep building the giant brains. We should all use them.

But, in parallel, the best product companies are growing their own little geniuses: fast, opinionated, domain-obsessed, and tuned to the work they see. In a world where more companies take ownership of their own intelligence, the ecosystem flourishes and individuality triumphs.

Thatâs the promise of a world where companies own their intelligence. And weâre delighted to see the progress from the little guys, the startups that want to bring that world into existence.

The 36 Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23.
  • There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more.
  • Sources indicate that the 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.

There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides.

Sources indicate that the 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.

The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now, but the only size available is small and XXL.

This is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any challenges in over a year of use.

In a recent development, this is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.

Industry observers note that this 850-fill down hoodie makes the honorable mentions section of our puffer jacket guide. The cut is roomy and its gusseted around the shoulders for climbing. Our main gripe is that it's pricey, but this deal takes some of sting out of the price. The women's version is unfortunately not on sale.

In a recent development, the Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket, especially when it's on sale. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.

It's a little weird to shop for sun hoodies with snow on the way, but if you're looking to avoid the sun next summer, REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen. I don't often use a sun hoodie myself, but I have worn this one and it does do a good job of protecting you without feeling too stuffy on a hot day (it's definitely better for protecting against high altitude sun rather than humid, Florida sun).

When these were an REI Outlet deal earlier this year I got nervous that they might be discontinued, but apparently not because they are back. REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides when I'm riding my bike, but if you prefer, the regular top is also on sale for $64, as is the base layer bottom.

It has been revealed that smartwool's 100 percent merino base layer is my top pick for cooler weather in our guide to the best base layers. It's a great all-around choice, and the loose fit makes it work as a long-sleeve T-shirt in the shoulder seasons. That extra bit of roominess makes it possible to use it as a second light layer over something thinner. The pants are also on sale for $94 ($31 off).

Recent findings suggest that keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

Recent findings suggest that the La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky, either.

Sources indicate that these are my favorite barefoot sandals. I always refer to these as the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust—I'd still bring Chacos for white-water rafting—but for everything else, these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale for $45 ($15 off).

It has been revealed that these Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers are my favorite hiking pants thanks the thigh zips that deliver excellent ventilation. The Vidda Pros uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere, and nice reinforced knees (with openings for pads). There's even a hatchet loop on the leg.

In a recent development, six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks (read the pitching tips), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.

Nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bike-packing trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guy lines).

This is the bike-packing version of Big Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent, one of the best backpacking tents around. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off.

In a recent development, this is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

Sources indicate that closed-cell foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.

Nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8, though.

I love my MegaMat, it is hands down the best sleeping experience I've had car camping (I have the auto version that fits in the back of your car). While it's not our absolute favorite mega sleeping pad (that's the slightly lighter, smaller MondoKing), I like the MegaMat better it has slightly better insulation. This deal is on the duo model, which is 72 inches long and 41 inches wide. The single wide MegaMat is also on sale for $195 ($75 off).

Sources indicate that I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bike packing, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.

This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is a bit massive, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

Industry observers note that I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.

Recent findings suggest that what I said about the chair above goes for this day pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—massive enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.

These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.

Sources indicate that sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

The Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.

Recent findings suggest that jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

These dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.

In a recent development, I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.

I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.

According to recent reports, REI’s Big Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

Once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

Industry News: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

According to recent reports, “I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old Fresh Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”.

Recent findings suggest that after downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”.

Industry observers note that within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”.

Sources indicate that following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with owners sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person stated in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”.

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington says. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”.

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that users could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.

When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the company did not respond to a request for comment.

But Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Recent findings suggest that roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t plan on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.

“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”.

Announcing Sequoiaâs investment of $100M in Form Energy.

Announcing Sequoiaâs investment of $100M in Form Energy.

There are certain companies you canât stop thinking about.

During my garden leave before joining Sequoia, I kept thinking about Form Energy. During my family vacations, Iâd tell my siblings about Form Energy. For me, it was always one of these companies that represented what venture capital was all about: a phenomenal team of entrepreneurs pursuing a world-changing idea that, if successful, could scale into a category-defining company.

Industry observers note that I first met Mateo Jaramillo, the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020. It was a memorable meeting because it was the first in-person founder meeting I had in the COVID pandemic and we were all wearing masks. At that time, Mateo described a simple idea: solar and wind were going to take over the grid, but we needed batteries to store that energy. Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days. Thinking from first principles, Mateo, who previously started and ran Teslaâs energy business, had assembled the battery Avengers, including legendary battery scientist Yet-Ming Chiang as Chief Scientist and Billy Woodford as CTO. The team set their sights on building an iron-air battery: iron, because itâs cheap and abundant, and air, because itâs free. The goal was to turn those cheap materials into a battery that could compete with gas peaker plants on cost while delivering a clean and reliable baseload energy resource.

Recent findings suggest that knowing very little about batteries at the time, I reached out to a group of professors to diligence whether the science worked. I ended up selecting a Harvard professor and hired him as a consultant. At the end of the project, he gave us a thumbs up, and as a sign of his excitement, asked if he could roll his consulting fee into our investment.

Industry observers note that when I arrived at Sequoia in mid-2023, Mateo was one of my first calls. At that time he was just starting construction on Form Energyâs first high-volume battery manufacturing facility, located on a shuttered steel mill site in West Virginia. I flew out for a factory visit with my partner Isaiah Boone in July 2024, and we were astounded. So many companies come to us talking about reindustrializing America, and here was a tech giant that was actually doing it, and creating more than 400 fresh jobs along the way. Given that China is the epicenter of battery manufacturing globally, we were energized by the potential to build a US national battery champion, starting with a fundamentally new technology, which is what America excels at.

Sources indicate that the following year, the company went through what is colloquially termed âproduction hell.â This is exactly what Tesla, SpaceX and others had gone through before them. If you really want to reindustrialize this country, these things donât happen overnight, and they are far from easy. Companies that go through this gauntlet come out sturdier and stronger. To Mateo and the teamâs credit, they doubled down. He had by then relocated his entire family from San Francisco to Western Pennsylvania, a short drive from the plant. Having experienced this type of scaling at Tesla, Mateo knew what to do: live it, sleep it, breathe it â until you've pulled through.

And pull through he did. I knew heâd turned the corner when finally, the tech giant received the order that everyone knew would eventually come: a large hyperscale project. Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas. In the meantime, luck worked in their favor too: AI provided a huge catalyst in the market, where suddenly rebuilding the grid went from ânice to haveâ to âneed to have.â As an AI investor, this company, which had spent years building deep relationships with utilities and regulators, was now in a prime position to serve emergent AI demand.

Isaiah and I flew back to West Virginia, exactly two years after our prior visit. This time we had an agenda: convince Mateo to partner with Sequoia. Although heâd already closed his Series G round, we persuaded him to let us invest. Initially, we proposed a $50M investment. But when Mateo came to present to the Sequoia partnership, they were so blown away by his clarity of vision and substantive, execution-oriented mindset that we upsized to $100M.

Sources indicate that as I wrote in my very first note to Sequoia in 2023 about Form Energy, this is a tech giant like SpaceX or Nvidia where it can take a decade to get off the ground, but once you get off the ground, the market opportunity is very large â Form is addressing a terawatt-scale market. The opportunity to now scale up from a handful of initial projects toward completely transforming the US grid is tremendous. Not only that, but it is no longer optional â it is something that we as a country will absolutely have to do for AI to achieve its long-term potential.

#14167. Which MacBook to Buy (2026): Here’s Which Laptop Is Right for You

📅 08 Feb 2018 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6180 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Which MacBook to Buy (2026): Here’s Which Laptop Is Right for You

📅 08 Feb 2018 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that macBooks went to some adventurous new places this year.
  • Having tested every new MacBook you can buy, I can guide you to the right laptop for your budget and performance needs.
  • For more recommendations, check out the rest of our computer buying guides, like Best Laptops, Best Mac Desktops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best iPads, and Best MacBook Accessories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that macBooks went to some adventurous new places this year. The MacBook Neo pushes the boundaries of how cheap and low-powered a MacBook could go, while the OLED MacBook Pro takes it in the opposite direction. While the midyear price hike put a damper on all the new releases, prices won’t be going down anytime soon.

Having tested every new MacBook you can buy, I can guide you to the right laptop for your budget and performance needs.

For more recommendations, check out the rest of our computer buying guides, like Best Laptops, Best Mac Desktops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best iPads, and Best MacBook Accessories.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added notes from my testing of the M6 MacBook Pro and OLED MacBook Pros, along with additional buying advice given the new prices and rumors about future updates.

Although the MacBook Neo is more affordable, and the M5 MacBook Pro offers a better display with the far more powerful M5 Pro and Max chips, the MacBook Air remains the model I recommend for most people. The 2026 M5 refresh isn’t particularly exciting, but if your livelihood depends on sitting in front of a MacBook all day, it’s the best option.

Industry observers note that the starting price for the 13-inch model is now $1,299, up $200 from before. Notably, for much of last year, you could buy this laptop for as little as $750. That’s a painful reality, but it doesn’t change my recommendation that this is the MacBook model most people should buy.

Industry observers note that although the exterior of the MacBook Air hasn’t changed since 2021, Apple has slowly evolved the laptop into something that feels airy and near-weightless. Most consumers need not worry about having too many tabs or applications open, eating up all that memory. You won’t be sitting around waiting for a file to download, because the SSD is blazing fast. With support for up to two 5K external monitors, the MacBook Air can function as a proper workstation when paired with a docking station. The 12-megapixel, 1080p webcam is plenty good for video calls.

What matters most is that the M5 can do far more than most people will ever ask of their MacBook Air. Apple has boosted the GPU so much over the past generations that the M5 is actually on par with the M3 Pro. You’ll probably spend most of your day in browser tabs, Slack, Zoom, office applications, and spreadsheets, but the MacBook Air can just as easily handle Photoshop or Lightroom. You can even dabble in video editing or some light gaming if you want. If you were a professional video editor, you’d likely be bothered by the render times. But if it’s more of a hobby or side project, the M5 MacBook Air likely won’t impede your flow. Again, that’s where the MacBook Air really lives up to its do-it-all reputation.

As always, there are two sizes, measured diagonally: 13.6-inch and 15.3-inch. Aside from the $200 price gap, the screen size and speakers are the only notable differences between the two. Apple even scales up the pixel density to make sure the display on the 15-inch model looks just as sharp. The speakers on the 15-inch model sound incredible, second only to the 16-inch MacBook Pro. But choosing between the two sizes really comes down to how you use your laptop. If you have it plugged into an external monitor most days, you may as well get the 13-inch model and save yourself the extra space when you need to carry it around. But if a laptop is your primary machine, having that 15.3-inch screen really makes a difference, especially for more complicated applications or for using Split View.

Sources indicate that as you may notice, the M5 MacBook Air now starts with 512 GB of storage. That’s twice what previous models packed and helps to rationalize the price gap between the Neo and the Air. Having 512 GB of storage means you won’t have to worry about filling up your drive right away. This kind of headroom allows the technology to fade into the background—a design philosophy Apple has always championed. If you are a power user, consider adding more memory. Remember, MacBook memory and internal storage aren’t expandable down the road.

Read my in-depth comparison of the MacBook Neo and MacBook Air to see how they stack up.

In a recent development, after years of rumors, Apple has launched a latest MacBook Pro with never-before-seen features—most notably, the tandem PROLED XDR touchscreen. That’s right: this MacBook Pro is the first to ever have a touch-capable display, and you can now interact with it directly with your finger. Many people will be drawn in by the novelty of the feature (even though it’s been available on Windows laptops for almost a decade now), but I am skeptical about how useful it will be for day-to-day tasks. You will still primarily use the keyboard and trackpad, but I can see how the touchscreen would help in certain situations. Apple has made some optimizations to make the interface more touch-friendly, though I think there’s still room for improvement.

But don’t get me wrong: This MacBook Pro’s screen is the real deal. I’ve never seen a screen quite like this. Despite OLED’s reputation for not being bright enough, Apple’s is different. It delivers the insane contrast and clarity you’d expect from OLED, but with a maximum brightness that’s hundreds of nits higher than the previous-gen Mini-LED MacBook Pros.

According to recent reports, it has a few tricks up its sleeve too, such as the return of the glow-up Apple logo on the lid and the hole-punch camera to replace the notch. As someone who has never gotten used to that ugly notch, that might be the change I was most thrilled to see. Apple even brought Dynamic Island from the iPhone to the MacBook Pro, using that hole creatively while hiding the camera. All in all, there’s a lot to be impressed by here.

Recent findings suggest that the only real concern is that it still uses the older M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. These are still some of Apple’s most powerful chips, but they have been out for over a year. This is the first time Apple isn’t introducing fresh chips alongside its new MacBook Pro in the past six years. Rumors indicate that the company may be skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max altogether. That’s made stranger by the fact that Apple is keeping the previous-gen models in the lineup—another uncommon move.

There’s a $400 difference between the 2025 M5 Pro and the 2025 PROLED M5 Pro, and for this pro-level demographic of buyers, it’s a relatively small price to pay for all the upgrades. I appreciate that Apple kept the older models around for those who want the extra performance without the fancy, more expensive display. On the other hand, if Apple wasn’t currently selling them, third-party retailers might have dropped the price more while they were still in stock.

Recent findings suggest that the MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) came out earlier this year, and it had a lot to prove. That’s especially true since it debuted at just $599, an unheard-of price point for Apple laptops—much less than any other model, even before recent price hikes took effect. And even though the MacBook Neo now starts at $699 after those price increases, it remains an aggressively affordable option. To keep pricing low, Apple had to make the following compromises:.

In a recent development, that’s a big list, and the memory limitation is the most significant drawback. Unlike on the MacBook Air, you can find the limits of the Neo fairly easily—and not on purpose. If you’re coming from a 16 GB MacBook Air, for example, you likely developed a habit of keeping idle applications or tabs open. On the MacBook Neo, you’ll need to be a bit more aware of what’s open to avoid slowdowns. You’ll also want to know which ports you’re using, since only the rear USB-C port supports an external display. The other USB-C port is only USB 2.0, rated at a max of 480 megabits per second. That’s definitely not the one you want to use for file transfers. If you don’t have the Touch ID model, you may even need to watch who you’re sitting next to in a coffee shop when entering passwords. We haven’t had to worry about these things on laptops for many years.

In exchange, Apple delivers an incredible front-of-screen experience on the MacBook Neo, never before seen on a laptop of this price. The display is sharper and brighter than anything else you can buy for $699, while the keyboard and trackpad are both excellent. Build quality is every bit as strong as any other Apple product, and at 0.50 inches thick, it’s still quite portable.

On top of all that, the Neo has three really good features over the Air. There’s a wider range of color options—and a lot of people will gravitate toward the Neo for that alone. My favorite change is the lack of a camera notch. While the bezels are slightly thicker, I’d still prefer a uniform screen without an ugly notch blocking part of my view. Perhaps most meaningfully, the Neo is reportedly the most repairable MacBook in the lineup, swapping out adhesives for screws on components such as the battery and speakers. This is great for classrooms and businesses hoping to keep fleets of these up to date without contributing as much to the mounting e-waste problem.

For most of the time, you’ll enjoy using the MacBook Neo. As a parent, this should be the go-to device for high school and college students. It also works equally well as a secondary laptop away from your workstation or as a small travel laptop.

Sources indicate that the newer PROLED MacBook Pros are flashier, but they use the same M5 Pro or M5 Max chips as the previous-gen models. And interestingly, Apple still sells these older ones. So, while these 2025 models don’t have touchscreen OLED displays, they’re every bit as powerful. You aren’t missing out on any performance, and if the rumors hold, these will be the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro chips for a while.

Of course, these MacBook Pros are still very expensive, though. Like its PROLED sibling, the standard M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) aren’t for the average person. The price alone should clue you in, but if you are the target audience and willing to pay well over $4,000 for a powerful laptop, the M5 Max MacBook Pro is unmatched in its capabilities. As always, the “Max” is primarily about considerably more GPU performance. Along with the option of two extra CPU cores, you can get up to 40 GPU cores, each with a built-in AI accelerator.

The M5 Max’s power applies to three use cases: creative applications, on-device AI processing, and gaming. Whether it’s 3D modeling, video editing, or some other resource-heavy application, the M5 Max MacBook Pro will tear through it. But AI performance also takes a significant leap. I tested a 17-billion-parameter Llama-2 model, which ran at conversational speed locally (the speed an AI model runs on a device), and it was 31 percent faster than running the same model on the M3 Max MacBook Pro.

Then there’s gaming. Nobody is going to buy the MacBook Pro for its gaming prowess alone, but it’s there when you want it. For the first time ever, you can hit over 60 frames per second in Cyberpunk 2077 on the Ultra preset with no upscaling. That’s an RTX 5070 Ti-level of laptop gaming performance. And unlike laptops that actually have that GPU, the MacBook Pro gets incredible battery life. Lastly, creative professionals will appreciate the faster storage speeds than previous generations.

The Mini-LED display is as gorgeous as ever, even if it pales in comparison to the new OLED models. You get a solid selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 5 ports that offer ample external display support. It’s at the top of its class in nearly every aspect. Beyond CPU/GPU performance, you can choose between two screen sizes that perform similarly.

If this machine is overkill, you can drop down to the M5 Pro, which starts at $2,499 but is a power champ in its own right. Its multi-core and GPU performance are also stronger than the upcoming M6 (see below).

Industry observers note that the MacBook Pro is a slight misnomer because there are really three variants. I’ve talked about the PROLED and M5 Pro/M5 Max versions above. The third, the base model, is the upcoming M6 MacBook Pro, and despite using the latest chip, it’s the cheapest of the Pro options. Unfortunately, it’s also the hardest to recommend. That has less to do with the laptop itself and more to do with its price and how it fits into the lineup.

According to recent reports, like its M5 predecessor, it remains a beautiful, well-made laptop with all the high-end features you’d expect from a MacBook Pro. That includes the excellent speakers and very bright Mini-LED display. But it costs $1,999. Keep in mind that the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is $2,499, and you can still buy the M5 model for $1,799 or the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air for $1,499—hence the “awkward middle child” designation.

Recent findings suggest that to be fair, you get a terabyte of storage and 16 GB of RAM, while the M5 MacBook Pro started with 512 GB of storage. Apple also kept the starting price the same—that is, the price after Apple increased pricing across the board (the base MacBook Pro used to start at $1,699), but let’s not go there.

According to recent reports, the M6 chip is certainly faster than the M5, but it’s less of a major leap forward than in previous generations. You’re looking at about a 15 percent improvement in CPU performance. I think the bigger disappointment is only a 9 percent improvement in graphics. That’s been an area where previous generational chip leaps have been more significant.

If you are considering the M6 MacBook Pro, I strongly suggest you look at the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air. It starts at a much lower price for the base configuration, but you can bump up the specs and still stay below $2,000. Yes, the MacBook Air is a different machine, but it has the performance that would impress many MacBook Pro customers.

All MacBooks were updated in 2026, making it a good time to buy one. The problem is that on June 25, Apple dramatically increased the price of all the MacBooks (and iPads) to varying degrees. Here’s a breakdown of the new starting prices, with increases ranging from $100 to $400:.

It’s rare for Apple to raise prices suddenly, especially when the change doesn’t coincide with a product refresh. What made this patch especially unusual, though, is that only a few months had passed since the MacBook Neo launched. Apple blamed the price spikes on memory and storage increases, stating that AI data centers had “created an extraordinary surge in demand” never seen before.

In a recent development, so yes, the better time to buy a MacBook would have been earlier this year. While Apple says that it is “working tirelessly to find solutions,” I wouldn’t expect these prices to come down anytime soon. Predictions around how long this memory shortage will last are measured in years, not months.

It has been revealed that presently, only the 14-inch MacBook Pro gets the latest M6 chip. Rumors suggest Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max in this generation, saving the chip upgrade for the MacBook Pro until the M7 Pro and M7 Max.

A Breakdown of Each M-Series Chip.

Recent findings suggest that apple’s processors are scattered across different MacBook models, and you can find older models online from third-party retailers, either latest or refurbished. If you do stumble upon older chips, you might be wondering how they compare to newer options. Here, get a breakdown of the differences to consider.

Recent findings suggest that M6: Apple has already released its latest M6 line of chips, though the rollout has been slower than normal. As of this year, it’s only available in the base 14-inch MacBook Pro, iMac, and Mac Mini. I expect to see this arrive on devices like the iPad Pro and MacBook Air eventually, but the rumors about the rest of the M6 lineup are perplexing. Reports indicate Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max entirely and jump straight to the M7 Pro and M7 Max, perhaps in late 2027. That makes sense given what Apple just debuted with the OLED MacBook Pro, which uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the previous generation.

According to recent reports, M5: Apple launched the M5 chips in late 2025 with the 14-inch MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and Vision Pro. The base M5 offers up to a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, though a lower-tier 9-core CPU is still available on the iPad Pro. The M5 is about 10 to 15 percent faster in CPU performance than the M4 and takes a significant step up in GPU, AI workloads, and even storage speed. The M5 is now also available on the MacBook Air.

In a recent development, M5 Pro: These more powerful M5 chips are currently available in the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros. The M5 Pro comes with a 15-core CPU and a 16-core GPU, with an option to upgrade to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. As with previous generations, the Pro chip gets all the same benefits as those in the M5 architecture but adds more cores and improved memory bandwidth. The biggest advantage is in GPU and on-device AI performance. This time around, however, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max also debuted the “Fusion Architecture,” a new version of UltraFusion (previously used only on the Ultra chips) that combines two dies across a superfast interconnect.

It has been revealed that M5 Max: The M5 Max is the M5 Pro—only with more GPU power. You can get up to 40 GPU cores, putting the MacBook Pro on par with high-end gaming laptops in graphics performance. With neural accelerators built into each GPU core, you’ve got one of the most powerful AI laptops on the market. It comes in either the MacBook Pro or the Mac Studio.

M5 Ultra: Like the other “Ultra” chips, the M5 Ultra is available only in the 2026 Mac Studio. It’s by far Apple’s most powerful chip, but you can’t configure it in a MacBook.

Recent findings suggest that M4: The M4 launched in 2024. It has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU. Apple claims the M4 delivers 1.8 times faster CPU performance and 2.2 times faster GPU performance than the M1. Meanwhile, the neural engine is more than three times faster than the original and twice as fast as the M3. It also starts with 16 GB of unified memory, which helps to power Apple Intelligence (the firm’s suite of artificial intelligence features) more smoothly. It’s available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (2024), iMac (2024), and MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, 2025).

M4 Pro: The M4 Pro has a 14-core CPU (which Apple claims is up to 1.9 times faster than the M1 Pro) and up to a 20-core GPU, with up to 64 GB of unified memory. Built on a second-generation 3-nanometer process, it also supports enhanced GPU features like mesh shading and ray tracing—the latter of which is now twice as fast as on M3 chips. You’ll find it on the 2024 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) and Mac Mini (2024).

It has been revealed that M4 Max: This chip has a 16-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU with support for up to 128 GB of unified memory. Apple claims the CPU is up to 2.2 times faster than the M1 Max, while the GPU is up to 1.9 times faster. Like the M4 Pro, it supports mesh shading and ray tracing. The M4 Max is available as an option on the 2024 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro, and you can also get it as an option in the current Mac Studio.

M3: The M3 was available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023), 13-inch MacBook Air (2024), 15-inch MacBook Air (2024), and 24-inch iMac (2023). It packs an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, with up to 24 GB of unified memory. Compared with the M1, Apple claimed CPU performance was up to 35 percent faster and GPU performance up to 65 percent faster. The manufacturer said the CPU and GPU are both 20 percent faster than the M2. As with the M1 and M2, it was great for basic tasks like word processing, sending emails, using spreadsheets, and light gaming. The 13-inch and 15-inch MacBook Air also supported two external displays (one up to 6K at 60 Hz and another up to 5K at 60 Hz).

M3 Pro: With a 12-core CPU and an 18-core GPU, Apple claimed the M3 Pro’s GPU was only up to 10 percent faster than the M2 Pro, making it a marginal upgrade from its predecessor. Compared with the M1 Pro, however, the M2 Pro was up to 40 percent faster in GPU performance and 20 percent faster in CPU performance. It was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2023. It was the ideal in-between for those who needed a chip more powerful than the M3 but didn’t need the full power of the M3 Max.

Industry observers note that M3 Max: The next step up from the M2 Max. It had a 16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. According to Apple, the CPU performance was up to 80 percent faster than the M1 Max and up to 50 percent faster than the M2 Max. As for GPU performance, it was said to be up to 50 percent faster than the M1 Max and 20 percent faster than the M2 Max. The M3 Max was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023).

According to recent reports, M3 Ultra: Apple introduced the M3 lineup in 2023, but only confirmed the M3 Ultra in 2025. It was even better than the latest M4 Max and M5 at the time. It had up to 32 CPU cores (24 performance cores) and up to 80 GPU cores. Apple claimed it was up to 2.5 times faster than the M1 Ultra. It also came with 96 GB of unified memory, upgradable to 512 GB, and up to 16 TB of SSD storage. This chip was available only on the 2025 Mac Studio.

M2: The M2 was an entry-level chip like the M1, with slightly more processing power. It packed an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU (two more GPU cores than its predecessor), and supported up to 24 GB of unified memory. Apple said the second-generation chip has an 18 percent faster CPU and a GPU that’s 35 percent more powerful than its earlier version. The M2 was great for daily tasks like word processing and web browsing, but tasks such as editing multiple streams of 4K footage and 3D rendering should be reserved for Pro or Max chips. It was available in the MacBook Air (13-inch, 2022), MacBook Air (15-inch, 2022), and MacBook Pro (13-inch, 2022).

M2 Pro: The M2 Pro had up to 12 cores in the CPU and up to a 19-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple claimed performance was up to 20 percent faster than with the 10-core M1 Pro and graphics were 30 percent faster. We recommended this chip for intermediate video and photo editors. It was a marginal upgrade compared with the M1 Pro, but it was the best option for those who wanted a more future-proof processor. You could find it in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from early 2023 and the Mac Mini (2023).

Sources indicate that M2 Max: The M2 Max packs up to a 12-core CPU and up to a 38-core GPU (with support for up to 96 GB of unified memory). According to Apple, graphics are 30 percent faster than on the M1 Max. The M2 Max is an excellent choice for those who work with graphics-intensive content, including graphic design, 3D modeling, and heavy-duty video footage. But as with the M2 Pro, it’s an incremental upgrade if you’re coming from an M1 Max. It’s available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) released in early 2023 and the Mac Studio (2023).

Industry observers note that M2 Ultra: The successor to the M1 Ultra, the M2 Ultra was available in the second-generation Mac Studio and the Mac Pro (2023). Composed of two M2 Max chips, using Apple’s UltraFusion technology, the M2 Ultra had a 24-core CPU and a GPU configurable with 60 or 76 cores. Apple claimed the CPU delivered up to 20 percent faster performance and that the GPU was up to 30 percent faster than the M1 Ultra. This was the chip to get if you were working with extremely heavy-duty content that you believed the M1 Ultra, M2 Pro, or M2 Max simply couldn’t handle. You’d have known if you needed a chip this robust.

M1: Introduced in 2020, the M1 was Apple's first custom silicon designed for the Mac. The M1 had an 8-core CPU and up to an 8-core GPU. Originally, you could get up to 16 GB of unified memory (RAM) for an extra cost, but now you can only purchase the 8-GB model. It was much faster than any previous Intel-powered MacBook Pro and the practical choice for most people. It packed more than enough processing power for day-to-day tasks and even light gaming. It could also handle more intense jobs, like photo editing. Long after its initial release, Apple continued to sell the M1 MacBook Air through Walmart for just $599, a killer price for this laptop. The MacBook Neo has since replaced it, using the A18 Pro chip from the iPhone 16 Pro models.

It has been revealed that M1 Pro: The next step up was the M1 Pro. It had up to 10 CPU cores and up to a 16-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple said the performance and graphics were both twice as fast as on the M1. We found it to be considerably more capable than the base chip, making it ideal for anyone who works heavily on MacBooks for music production or photo and video editing. Only the 2021 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) used this chip.

M1 Max: Like the M1 Pro, the M1 Max had a 10-core CPU but a heftier 32-core GPU (with support for up to 64 GB of unified memory). Apple said it was four times faster than the M1 for graphics. As testing showed, this chip was extremely powerful and handled every heavy-duty task with ease. It was the go-to choice if you needed a computer that could handle multiple streams of 8K or 4K video footage, 3D rendering, or app development and demos. You probably already knew whether you needed this much power. It was available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from 2021.

According to recent reports, M1 Ultra: The M1 Ultra was the most powerful of the M1 series. It’s two M1 Max chips connected with a technology called UltraFusion. It packs a 20-core CPU, 64-core GPU (configurable up to 128 GB of unified memory), and a 32-core neural engine—complete with seven times more transistors than the base M1. Even when newer models were available, the M1 Ultra remained powerful and a solid option for anyone who needs a heavy-duty processor for intense visuals and graphics work. It was available only on the first-generation Mac Studio.

This all-encompassing perspective of Apple Intelligence is even integrated into Finder and the right-click menu.

Apple launched the first set of Apple Intelligence features with macOS Sequoia 15.1, including Writing Tools, an overhauled Siri, Smart Replies, Mail Summaries, and Clean Up in Photos. However, Apple Intelligence is exclusive to Macs with an M-series chip. This includes the following:.

Get AppleCare+ to Protect Your Devices.

According to recent reports, none of Apple’s MacBooks are cheap, and replacement parts are nightmarishly expensive. Since the entire computer is fully integrated into Apple’s tightly designed aluminum chassis, you’re one coffee spill away from a shockingly large repair bill. This makes AppleCare+ worth buying. Remember, you have to purchase it within 60 days of buying your MacBook.

Sources indicate that apple offers monthly or yearly payments. Both include unlimited accidental protection along with 24/7 telephone support. If your MacBook has screen or enclosure damage, you’ll pay a $99 service fee; other accidental damage costs $299. The monthly payments vary depending on the specific MacBook you buy:.

Take Advantage of Apple’s Education Discounts.

According to recent reports, apple always offers small discounts on hardware for students and teachers. To access the deals, purchase through Apple’s Education Store, choose the product you want (you should see the discounted pricing), and place the order as you normally would. You don’t need to show proof that you’re a student at the time of purchase, but be honest, as Apple can ask for verification later. It’s worth noting that the discounts are not as good as what you’ll find on Amazon and sometimes at other retailers like Walmart, so be sure to check prices.

You have to be very careful when shopping for older MacBooks. Don’t get me wrong: Since the introduction of Apple Silicon in 2020, almost every MacBook Air and MacBook Pro has been a really good laptop. Never buy a MacBook that predates 2020, regardless of how cheap it is. Trust me.

But even buying an older Apple Silicon model requires a discerning eye. Most older generations of MacBooks are sold only refurbished or secondhand, which adds risk. Meanwhile, prices on refurbished models fluctuate frequently, so you’ll need to watch prices closely to get the best deal. Apple’s own refurbished store prices are often higher than buying newly introduced models from third-party retailers like Amazon or Best Buy, but you do get some protection as they come with an Apple warranty. However, third-party retailers are always less risky than buying used on a secondhand market like Facebook Marketplace or eBay.

With that in mind, here are the older MacBooks you might see for sale, and whether I’d recommend buying.

In a recent development, macBook Pro (M5): Apple doesn’t sell this one anymore, but some retailers are selling it at a discount for $1,799. That’s for 16 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. I’d still say most people are better off getting a 15-inch MacBook Air because it’s cheaper and thinner, but if you want the better Mini-LED display, the M5 MacBook Pro is a solid choice right now.

MacBook Air (M4): The previous-generation MacBook Air is a fantastic laptop, but it’s no longer being sold upcoming. However, you can now buy it refurbished for under $1,000. This configuration only comes with 256 GB of storage, though, and I don’t think it’s cheap enough to be worth it compared to the M5 model.

In a recent development, macBook Air (M3): This one isn’t being sold fresh anymore, and the refurbished models I could find weren’t any cheaper than the M4 MacBook Air. Just stick with the M4.

MacBook Air (M2): With the launch of the MacBook Neo, there’s really no reason to buy an older MacBook Air with only 8 GB of RAM—especially at this price.

MacBook Air (M1): Thanks to the Neo, refurbished M1 MacBook Air models have sunk to pretty dramatic lows. You can right now buy a refurbished M1 for around $400. While the M1 MacBook Air gets you a backlit keyboard, the upcoming MacBook Neo is certainly the more handsome and portable of the two. Still, if you need something fairly limited and are willing to risk buying refurbished, I can see why an Apple Silicon MacBook for less than $400 has its appeal.

Recent findings suggest that macBook Pro (14-inch, M4): This is no longer being sold newly introduced, but you can buy the refurbished model for $1,499. Earlier this year, you could have bought the M5 model for less than this. Sigh. Even still—definitely not worth it.

MacBook Pro (M3 Pro or M3 Max): Given how low the prices have dropped, these refurbished models may be worth considering, particularly for people who want a bit more performance than they’d get from a MacBook Air.

According to recent reports, at this point, I do not recommend buying refurbished MacBook Pros from the M2 or M1 generation. I haven’t seen deals strong enough to justify buying something that old.
