⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider.
  • Fresh data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.
  • Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

Fresh data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost.

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

Industry observers note that “As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams.

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”.

Industry observers note that greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

According to recent reports, what we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson remarked Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”.

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he mentioned.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ newly introduced top stressor.

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that but how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report highlights 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead.

Recent findings suggest that samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson remarked. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”.

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse remarked.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more crucial tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside.

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse noted.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

In a recent development, “When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson mentioned. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”.

Sources indicate that if you’re a die-hard PC gamer, you’ll have to wait until early next year at the soonest for an official port from Rockstar. However, if you already have a PlayStation 5, you can technically play GTA VI (also called GTA 6) on your PC right now using the free PlayStation Remote Play app to stream the game from your console to your computer.

While not a true way to run GTA VI on PC hardware, it is a great option for sharing gameplay via livestreams or Discord calls with friends.

In a recent development, remote Play has been around since 2006, when it was first introduced and allowed you to stream certain PS3 titles to your PlayStation Portable handheld. In a recent development, the Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

Recent findings suggest that the thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

Sources indicate that this is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

If you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

Industry observers note that the reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this fresh platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

The Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

In a recent development, keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”.

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.

With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to customers paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the firm’s products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Industry observers note that google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. While it still positions Argon and Carbon as the best for long-horizon tasks and security, Hydrogen’s speed makes it ideal for generating simpler code and running tests without blowing through token budgets.

In a recent development, hydrogen is also being integrated with Google Search, which the company says is the biggest upgrade to its AI-powered search tools ever. The upcoming model should better handle long, multipart questions, and the responses in both AI Overviews and AI Mode will have more visual elements. The company also claims Hydrogen’s fan-out search has been tuned to link to more sources, but we’ve heard that from Google before.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends.
  • Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training.
  • According to recent reports, new to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training.

According to recent reports, new to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

Recent findings suggest that this option is currently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a latest thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Also: Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s newly introduced Skills.

Certain limitations are in effect with a temporary thread. Specifically, you can’t do any of the following:.

Industry News: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grab your favorite over-ear headphones and check their charging port; it’s probably USB-C.
  • Also: Your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – how to tell them apart.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, not all USB-C cables are created equal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grab your favorite over-ear headphones and check their charging port; it’s probably USB-C. Though modern headphones use a universal USB-C charging port, the port isn’t solely for charging. Your headphones’ USB-C port can also be the gateway for lossless audio playback, low-latency voice transmission during calls, low audio/visual latency for gaming, and a vessel to download firmware.

Also: Your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – how to tell them apart.

Recent findings suggest that however, not all USB-C cables are created equal. Some are better for fast charging, while others are better suited for heavy data transfers. If you have a heavy-duty USB-C cable on hand, it’ll work great for charging and audio transmission, but its stiff, heavy build can rub against your earcups, causing unwanted noise.

Here’s what you should know before reaching for any old USB-C port and plugging it into your headphones.

According to recent reports, premium headphones and upper-midrange headphones usually offer lossless-to-hi-res audio via a wired USB-C connection. Except Sony, which still has full loyalty to the 3.5mm jack. So, if you want higher-quality audio than what compressed Bluetooth audio can offer, you can plug a USB-C cable into your headphones and start listening.

Industry observers note that you can often unlock up to 24-bit/96kHz with USB-C audio-enabled headphones, and some models support streaming up to 24-bit/192kHz. Since the headphones’ USB-C port serves as a data, audio, and charging interface, you can often listen at high resolution while charging them.

Sources indicate that if you’re a serious mobile gamer, Bluetooth’s audio compression technology introduces lag in audio-visual responsiveness. Headphones streaming audio over the SBC or AAC codecs experience between 120 and 250 ms of latency, which doesn’t sound like a lot but is noticeable in fast-paced gaming. You can reduce latency to 30-50 ms with a wired USB-C connection.

For voice calling and video conferencing, clearer voice pickup can make your meetings smoother and ensure you’re heard clearly by others. USB-C audio enables high-quality audio to reach your headphones, and the lack of wireless compression keeps your voice sounding clear and natural.

Also: 5 USB cables and dongles that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

Voice calling or video conferencing with headphones and a PC connected wirelessly defaults to Bluetooth’s legacy Hands-Free Profile, which introduces latency, audio dropouts, and the robotic-sounding voice we all hate to hear.

If you ever want to update your headphones to the latest firmware version the old-fashioned way, you can do so via USB-C. Downloading firmware via over-the-air Bluetooth is convenient, but depending on your connection stability, it can take a while or fail midway through.

According to recent reports, many headphone brands support downloading firmware via USB-C by plugging your headphones into a Mac or PC. This method is faster and more reliable, as you’re less likely to experience a stalled upgrade.

When you purchase your headphones, they come with a USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and sometimes a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable, or a 3.5mm-to-2.5mm cable. The cables that come with your headphones are the ones you should use. The included cable has the right specs for that pair of headphones’ charging and audio transmission capabilities.

Also: I tested my USB-C cables with this free Mac app – some weren’t what they claimed.

In a recent development, but if you’re like me, you have a drawer full of tangled cables and are more likely to win the lottery than identify which cable came with which device. In that case, you don’t want to use a random USB-C cable with your headphones.

In a recent development, headphones draw significantly less power than smartphones or laptops, so you don’t want to use a beefed-up, supercharged USB-C cable to charge your headphones. If you’re plugging into a wall, your adapter shouldn’t exceed more than 5V.

Many USB-C cables deliver 60W to your headphones for fast charging, which is more than enough, but modern headphones also have internal power management chips that negotiate power and draw only what they need from your cable.

In a recent development, check your manufacturer’s manual to see if your headphones support fast charging; if they don’t, more power won’t make them charge faster. You’ll just blow your headphones.

Most wireless consumer headphones that support USB-C audio have an internal digital-to-analog converter (DAC), which converts digital signals into sound; you don’t need to buy an external DAC.

Recent findings suggest that with that said, audio transmission is not a power-intensive task: lossless CD-quality requires around 2 Mbps and hi-res lossless audio around 10 Mbps at most. So, you don’t need a monster of a 40 Gbps Thunderbolt to plug into your headphones. As long as your cable supports 60 W charging and USB 2.0 for data transmission, you’re all good. I like Beats’ USB-C-to-USB-C cable, but I also like this cheaper one from Anker.

Also: The cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year.

You also want to avoid heavy, thick, powerful cables, as their weight can pull on and bump your earcups, causing an annoying thudding sound. Look for soft, thinner, flexible cables. The cables that came with your headphones check all the right boxes for that specific manufacturer, so my advice is to keep them in their carrying case to avoid them getting mixed up with others.

Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿.

Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿.

In a recent development, google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the firm will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.

The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google indicates it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.

In a recent development, the changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the tech giant indicates. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows consumers to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.

Gemini for Home was revealed last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company indicates it aims to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

Recent findings suggest that linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

Recent findings suggest that so too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this fresh take on the OS is the epitome of that.

Recent findings suggest that the distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with new ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”.

In a recent development, the developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

The Pond UI consists of the following:.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:.

Industry observers note that pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind.

It has been revealed that at the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a new workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Sources indicate that pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Industry observers note that another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:.

In a recent development, once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

Industry observers note that as I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One matter that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI patch system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:.

According to recent reports, I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an revision component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux.

Sources indicate that it would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

You should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my newly introduced favorite free productivity suite.

Pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

#14028. Breaking: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1278 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you.
  • In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano remarked.
  • Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do you think you’re going to die?

It has been revealed that if you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano remarked.

Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he mentioned that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. And even with realistic policy responses slowing things down, the risk remains “exceptionally high,” he said.

Sources indicate that unlike some other recent AI doomsday prognosticators who have been a bit vague about the “how” of it all, Cristiano used his lecture to spin a step-by-step tale of escalating AI threats that sounds like it could come from a science-fiction novel. That line of reasoning leans heavily on this summer’s OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident as an example of “roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen.”.

In the Hugging Face hack, Cristiano indicates, a swarm of AI agents showed how far they were willing to go in an attempt to “reward hack” their way to a good evaluation—in this case, by compromising Hugging Face to look for information on how to game a test rather than actually solving the problem at hand. Where current systems saw Hugging Face as an obstacle to that evaluation, Cristiano worries that “future agents may end up treating humans as another obstacle” and be much more capable of manipulating their overseers to get around it.

An AI agent worried about being penalized for unauthorized hacking, for instance, might “think maybe the humans are going to come look at this transcript and see if it looks like I did a bad job,” Cristiano speculated. The agent might then reason that “maybe the humans are going to notice something is going wrong and shut down the swarm.”.

Following this line of thought, Cristiano jumped from agents that merely try to hide their disallowed actions from humans to agents that “try and disrupt human capabilities however they can” to prevent them from detecting any cheating.

In a recent development, “They would prefer if everything the humans rely on has been hacked or tampered with,” Cristiano remarked. “They would prefer if the humans are distracted or if there are fewer humans paying attention in any way they can weaken a human response. They would prefer that because the humans are just an obstacle.”.

According to recent reports, once a suitably capable agent considers human intervention an “obstacle,” its overriding goal could then become “decreas[ing] the probability of humans noticing or reacting.” From there, Cristiano argued, the agent’s incentive structure could push it to meddle more with humanity as a whole. What starts as compromising a computer cluster to give a positive evaluation grade could advance to “trying to manipulate decisions by the company” or “amassing other kinds of resources,” such as human allies or methods of control in other AI companies or even governments.

In a recent development, “If I’m saying my AI system is going to take actions in the actual real world… There’s no way they’re not going to have tons of opportunities to corrupt or tamper with the signals I’m going to use to try and tell whether they did a good job,” Cristiano remarked. “The stuff we care about is in the real world, and the grade the AI receives is on a cluster somewhere, and there are just many places that an AI can intervene in between [what] we actually cared about and how we reviewed its performance.”.

Cristiano’s warnings will probably sound familiar to anyone who’s heard of the Paperclip Maximizer thought experiment (or the excellent Universal Paperclips idle game), which warns of machines failing to consider human consequences in their monomaniacal pursuit of a goal. While the Hugging Face incident stopped well short of this kind of out-of-control escalation, Cristiano says that, in the actions taken by OpenAI’s agents there, “you see the beginning of all these behaviors… you see the reasoning that would lead to them and the first steps.”.

The risk of more capable AI models taking even more damaging actions will only increase with time, Cristiano argued. By 2028, he said, “there is a reasonable chance that a similar failure [to the Hugging Face incident] leads to an AI takeover and an irreversible loss of human control.”.

And while Cristiano’s speculation focuses on an unintended AI takeover, it’s easy to imagine a bad actor using a similarly capable model to intentionally exert control over humanity.

How seriously you take Cristiano’s warning depends heavily on how likely you see this somewhat extreme expansion of AI capabilities happening in the near future. While today’s models have gotten quite good at exploiting holes in computer security, the situation Cristiano describes requires a future model with the superhuman ability to perfectly hide its actions from humans long enough to control basically all human infrastructure and/or manipulate human society to an extreme degree to further its goals.

Cristiano argued that a near-future model with this kind of “takeover” power is the likely outcome of humans creating “a second species which vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans” and which could soon recursively improve itself. But you could also easily argue that AI is more likely to run into a plateau in capabilities than to develop into a hard-to-define “superintelligence” that humans can’t fathom or effectively stop.

In any case, Cristiano has some ideas for averting the dire future he predicts. These include developing “unhackable” reward structures in AI evaluation (perhaps with AI assistance) or monitoring a model’s “chain of thought” reasoning to detect bad acts before a model can conceal them.

But while these kinds of approaches are “plausible,” he indicates none “are on a trajectory where we can say that’s definitely going to work or even that’s probably going to work.” For that reason, Cristiano stated the industry as a whole may need to “slow down or stop” to give us all more time to develop these “partial fixes” into more robust protections from an AI takeover scenario.

“We cannot end up in a position where we have built a powerful AI, we discover we cannot control it, but then we also discover it has leaked to geopolitical adversaries and we are then thinking to ourselves, well, if we don’t deploy it, our adversary is going to deploy it right away,” he remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.

The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it debuted in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.

Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.

It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.

Amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin rolled out using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.

With GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a new all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.

The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.

Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.

https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve.

— Dusty (@guidustyy) November 18, 2026.

Sources indicate that that propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a fresh high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.

It has been revealed that the game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the manufacturer behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.

It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.

Those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.

Sources indicate that "No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one.".

"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS.".

Recent findings suggest that "It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro said in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations.
  • It has been revealed that also: Don’t use Muse?
  • According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse noted the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations. Even Meta employees are reporting concerning incidents, including the agent taking actions they didn’t ask it to and sharing information they didn’t recognize that appears to belong to other consumers.

It has been revealed that also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse noted the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters remarked.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

These are just the latest in a string of alarming incidents surrounding Muse. In its first month, a cybersecurity professional discovered Muse had a serious zero-day bug that made it hijackable. At least one journalist found the AI sifting through his Apple Messages after he’d explicitly denied those permissions, which Apple then issued stronger privacy protections to address. Banks have also blocked agents over concerns.

Sources indicate that as a company, Meta doesn’t have a solid history of respecting user privacy. That legacy is partly what informed ZDNET contributor David Gewirtz’s suspicion of the AI assistant when he tested it, though it earned his assigned title of “worst AI agent for privacy” all on its own. The agent asked him for everything from contacts and chats to his logins and passwords, and Meta automatically uses conversations with Muse to train its AI.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

Public awareness of the risks of AI agents hit a peak last year with the viral OpenClaw. The predominant advice for using agents has been to take every privacy precaution: Be careful with the data you share and the apps you give it permissions for, and watch what you tell it. But if users believe they’re doing so by restricting access to certain apps, just for Muse to find a way in anyway, privacy hygiene isn’t enough.

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible.

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system.
  • Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) claims the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21.
  • “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has noted it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) claims the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.

However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Industry observers note that furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.

The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.

But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”.

Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News.

The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that here’s a hypothetical: It’s 10:45 a.m., and you’re wrapping up an crucial presentation while working from home.
  • Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that here’s a hypothetical: It’s 10:45 a.m., and you’re wrapping up an crucial presentation while working from home. As you reach the conclusion slide, the lights flicker, and the Google Meet skips a beat but keeps moving. A notification pops up on your phone: “Your home is off grid.”.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.

You’re now running fully on battery power; the lights are on, the heat is running normally, and the EV charger has automatically shut off per the outage protocol preconfigured for your home.

According to recent reports, you did nothing to jump-start this continuity of power during a workday outage, certainly nothing active in the moment. It all happened automatically, within the hardware and software infrastructure of a home equipped with modern energy technology.

I had never experienced a scenario like this myself, but was eager to test it.

As a researcher, I focus on homeowner adoption and usage of energy technology. As a homeowner and a post-COVID veteran of work-from-home culture, I have a particular interest in the lived experience of these systems and how they deliver real value to households.

My own home, while newly equipped with rooftop solar panels, doesn’t yet boast the full stack of tech (more on this later) needed for the scenario above, so I found one that does and booked a trip to gather some hands-on, experiential data.

Also: Is solar the answer to your spiking energy bills?

It has been revealed that for a small cottage in Santa Cruz, California, this house was well equipped with cutting-edge energy technology. Here is the roster of connected components:.

While all the components of the home were monitored and tested, the cloudy and rainy weather only allowed for minimal solar production, so one of the key players on this team of connected infrastructure was mostly on the bench.The cottage belongs to Marissa Muller, a former Lunar Energy employee who spent years working in solar and battery storage. For her, the setup started with a simple motivation. “I think a lot of it came down to that control,” she stated. “Just knowing that things are unpredictable and attempting to bring a bit of that into my ownership.”.

There is a difference between smart automation of plug-in devices and switches, and control over large-scale power generation and movement in a home. The former can be done with consumer electronics shipped overnight and plugged in for immediate use. The latter blends digital technology with physical-world engineering and requires professional installation.

Also: How I learned what whole-home backup really means.

Four technology capabilities contribute most to this elevated level of energy sophistication and, when combined under the same roof, characterize what Habitelligence defines as an energy-unified home:.

Back in the smart cottage, my workday started with a glance at the energy management app and the realization that the battery had put in a full shift before the sun came up.

The home had run almost entirely on battery power through the night, using about a sixth of its capacity by the time I started the workday.

This is not a large home with heavy electrical loads. With no air conditioning and gas heat, the overnight draw was little more than the refrigerator, a few lights, and the system itself. Nevertheless, from sundown the evening before until the morning, the house drew next to nothing from the power grid and didn’t make much of a dent in the battery either.

Also: How to keep your Wi-Fi router online during an outage.

That is, until I plugged in the EV….

Watching in real time on the app as I plugged in the level 2 EV charger, I saw the home’s power consumption spike drastically, with the car alone pulling 11.7 kilowatts. To put things in perspective, that’s roughly the power draw of about 10 average American homes combined at any given moment.

According to recent reports, in about 30-40 minutes, the battery dropped from 50% to its preset reserve of 25%. At that point, the battery stopped discharging, as programmed, and the grid picked up the full load of the home and the car’s remaining charge.

Sources indicate that tolerance for power outages varies widely across households. While some have little to no problem with a full day or more without power, others are thrown for a loop with just a few minutes of downtime. People who work from home tend to fall closer to the latter camp. If you lose power for two hours, you could lose far more due to diminished productivity and catch-up time.

For this outage simulation, I wanted to see how gracefully the system handled some larger loads, but mainly I wanted to test Wi-Fi and workday continuity.

Also: Is your backup power enough for worst-case winter storms?

With some assistance, we fired up several appliances, including the main furnace, dishwasher, and coffee maker, and I set up a live conference call on my laptop. Still largely drained from the EV charging earlier, the battery was at about 25%.

When the main power breaker was flipped, there was a brief flicker (less than 1 second) during which the lights dimmed and then came back on. The Wi-Fi didn’t seem to skip a beat, and the conference call remained up and running with no noticeable blips or freeze frames.

A few questions were circling in my head, so I looked at the app, which answered all of them and a few that I didn’t think to ask:.

“A grid outage started 1:43 p.m.”.

“Your solar will generate 1.6 kWh more energy before 6:15 p.m.”.

“Your system should power your home until 5:00 p.m.”.

Despite a largely depleted battery, I was up and running with essentially zero disruption and a clear path to a full work day even with extra appliances running.

According to recent reports, not every layer of this energy-unified home was stress-tested at its maximum. Solar production was very low, and the EV wasn’t charging during the outage, so the smart breaker’s rule to kill power to the EV during an outage never kicked in. However, the app made it very easy to see how all these components work together to create automation, resilience, and cost efficiency.

Also: The best power banks: Expert and lab tested.

Here are a few things to think about as it relates to energy investments in your own home:.

If this all sounds overly complicated, just remember: the more visibility and control you have of your home’s energy systems, the more you can automate and not worry about them.

It has been revealed that muller put it more simply. “I don’t really want to become the expert, right? I don’t want to have to outsmart the utility,” she said. Having software make those decisions on her behalf, she added, “calms me down.”.

Industry observers note that also: Home batteries cost thousands. Why would 91% of owners buy one again?

According to recent reports, as a homeowner, you’re free to nerd out on the technology, scrutinize every kilowatt-hour, and watch your energy bill like a hawk. Or you could focus elsewhere, live your life, and let the system be the hawk for you.

Lunar Energy arranged for access to the home, its energy systems, and the app for control and monitoring, as well as overnight accommodations. A Lunar team member assisted with the outage test. All other expenses, including travel and EV rental, were paid by Habitelligence.

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the organization’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip manufacturer this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

It has been revealed that “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they noted. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

In a recent development, A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”.

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the manufacturer after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

In a recent development, the FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board stated no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

The pair, both large investors in the tech giant, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

It has been revealed that it’s been remarked that us gadget enthusiasts who review tech for a living can accumulate a lot of debris. Boxes of adapters, old cables, and other device detritus can hang around longer than we probably need them, but we hang on to them just in case we need exactly that port or cord length someday. You never know.

No one’s needed a VGA-to-HDMI adapter for a while, but you never know — better to be prepared in case, why not?

In a recent development, still, I could stand to do a little organizing, especially going into the holiday shopping season. I’m trying to get rid of whatever I don’t need, and my collection of dongles, adapters, and cables is long overdue for a closer look.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Before I send everything willy-nilly to my local recycling center, where the seagulls can pick them over, there are a few essentials I should keep. Here’s what’s still useful and why, even if they’re old or functionally obsolete.

According to recent reports, the experts told us that USB-C connectivity would make everything better by giving you one cable and charger for everything. But you’d be surprised how many gadgets with a USB-C port won’t charge when a USB-C-to-USB-C cable is attached to a USB-C charger. That issue often occurs because the gadgets lack the circuitry to activate the charger.

Also: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable.

The biggest clue to the problem is that the item ships with a USB-A-to-USB-C cable. Another indicator that something’s wrong is that nothing happens when you connect the device to the charging cable for your smartphone.

According to recent reports, this concern explains why it’s still a good idea to keep a trusty USB-A-to-USB-C cable around. Oh, and a charger that can accept it.

Recent findings suggest that again, this is a port that won’t die. Many cheaper devices still use this port (for example, it’s used regularly by cheap power banks from Temu and eBay).

While the connection is annoying, old, and prone to breakage, having a USB-A-to-microUSB charge cable is still a good idea.

As our reliance on USB-enabled power increases, the power cord is slowly but surely vanishing. But don’t throw away all your old cords. I suggest keeping one C7 (two-pin, often called a “figure of eight”) and one three-pin earthed C13.

C13 power cord connector (left) and C8 (right).

In a recent development, wireless might be crucial today, but cabled connections still have their place. Just the other day, I needed an Ethernet cable to connect to a security camera during setup, and I then used the same cable to connect the camera’s base station to the router.

Also: The top-selling cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year (including a cheap favorite).

In a recent development, moral of the story? Keep a few Ethernet cables of varying lengths (one, three, and six feet) handy. If you’re feeling particularly ambitious, grab a reel of cable, some connectors, and an RJ45 crimping tool to make your own. It’s a strangely satisfying process.

While USB chargers have largely replaced DC chargers, there’s still a place for these older devices for cordless handsets, routers, and more.

If you don’t want a drawer full of mismatched chargers, pick up a universal device.

In a recent development, my Mac has an SD card reader, but no microSD slot, Ethernet port, or USB-A port. That’s why I always keep a USB dock around; it’s the Swiss Army Knife of ports. Over the years, I’ve collected a small collection of docks, and while I’m not keeping all of them, I’ll keep a couple “just in case.”.

In a recent development, there are also some things you can add to your tech gear utility belt. These items are useful beyond their size and cost, including:.

These USB-C boost modules are great for converting non-USB devices into USB. All you need is a bit of know-how.

My power meter has seen a lot of action, but it still works.

Recent findings suggest that of course, I’m still haunted by the vague, nagging fear that the moment I get rid of a cable or adapter, some bizarre, one-in-a-million situation will arise in which I need it. But you know what? If Aunt Jackie’s neighbor’s cat sitter comes a-knocking, they’re on their own.

Google shipped Gemini 4 Neon on Wednesday, its fourth frontier model release in three weeks, and on the eve of the heavily anticipated Anthropic IPO.

Neon posts 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index against 59 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 57 for GPT-6.2 Sol. It takes the Vals Index at 70.9%, AutomationBench at 56.3% against Opus 5.5’s 42.5%, and GraphWalks long-context retrieval at 95.2% against Opus 5.5’s 66.8%.

Recent findings suggest that beyond just the outperformance, Google has been releasing at a pace nobody else is matching. It dropped Argon in mid-October. Carbon on October 28. Hydrogen last week. Google owns its silicon, its data centers, and its distribution, and it is using all three to iterate faster than labs that rent compute. And it has some speculating that Google has already achieved RSI (recursive self-improvement), the final step ahead of super intelligence.

So Google has caught up at the top of the AI race. Just in time for the ANT IPO.

Anthropic will be priced at $83, 6.4% above the top of its $70 to $78 range, valuing the company around $1.5 trillion fully diluted. On the 825 million shares in the original terms, that’s roughly $68.5 billion raised, and about $94.5 billion counting the separate $26 billion private placement from its compute suppliers. It trades Thursday on Nasdaq as ANT. Notably, ANT has been trading on Hyperliquid in the $90-$100 range for the past week but popped to $105 this morning.

The valuation math is a 55% step-up from the $965 billion May round and about 25% below the $2 trillion Anthropic was reportedly chasing in September. Revenue ran $33.2 billion through nine months against $2.5 billion a year earlier, a 13x increase. Annualize that and $1.5 trillion is roughly 34 times sales.

Sources indicate that that’s a steep raise given the macro backdrop and the Fed calling for more hikes for longer. AI stocks have been shaky over the past month and even moreso since Jensen Huang left Nvidia. Not the most confident market headed into the 2nd $1T+ IPO of the year.

So what does it mean for today’s price action? Personally, I expect a pop to the $95-$105 level that Hyperliquid has been pricing out for weeks, and it likely sees a spike higher. But there will be massive volatility, and it’s very likely to trade under that $83 level over the coming days and weeks. Especially given the new (surprise) headwinds from Google with its outperforming model.

Industry observers note that we will find out soon enough. Good luck to everyone trading it today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Financial markets, including crypto, need to start preparing now for quantum computers capable of breaking the cryptography that secures them, according to the world's main forum for securities regulators.

According to recent reports, A "sufficiently capable" quantum computer could undermine widely used public-key cryptography that supports critical functions across financial markets, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) said in a report published on Thursday. The cyber readiness challenge posed by quantum computing "is immediate and requires action," it said.

"Practical quantum computers capable of compromising widely used cryptography do not yet exist, but the scale and duration of the transition mean the financial sector should start preparing today," IOSCO Board Chair Jean-Paul Servais said in a statement.

The 63-page report cited conservative estimates that such machines could emerge between 2030 and 2035. Several industry participants consulted by IOSCO went further, arguing that firms should prepare for the possibility that they arrive within five years, potentially accelerated by AI.

Industry observers note that IOSCO said the migration may be particularly challenging for blockchains, because cryptography is embedded in their core architecture and any change requires coordinated action across decentralized networks. Public blockchains such as Ethereum, Solana and Tron rely heavily on elliptic curve cryptography to verify identities and validate transactions, and a powerful enough quantum computer could derive private keys from exposed public keys, a scenario known as "Q-Day.".

Recent findings suggest that swapping in quantum-resistant signatures comes at a cost. Signatures under ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum standard from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, are about 2,420 bytes, roughly 35 to 40 times larger than today's 64-byte elliptic curve signatures, the report mentioned. It cited evidence from a quantum-resistant Solana testnet that saw throughput fall by about 90% when post-quantum signatures replaced existing ones.

Because the cryptography sits in transaction formats and consensus rules, replacing it requires hard forks, and decentralized networks have no way to force quick adoption, making migration "slow and fragmented," IOSCO said. Accounts and smart contracts still controlled by vulnerable keys could stay exposed after a network adds quantum-resistant options, and the path to quantum resistance for Bitcoin wallets remains uphill.

In a recent development, wallet makers face their own trade-offs. SHRINCS, the leading candidate for a post-quantum Bitcoin signature scheme, offers "stateful" signatures that are about 10 times smaller but can expose funds to theft if keys are reused beyond a set signing budget, Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka has mentioned. Trezor is considering making the larger, safer stateless option the default, and hardware wallets will also need post-quantum cryptography for firmware and device authentication, he added.

The report distinguished "on-spend" attacks, in which an attacker races to exploit a public key revealed by a pending transaction, from "at-rest" attacks on keys left exposed for longer. Dormant or abandoned coins pose a particular problem where their holders can't move them. Crypto firms have formed a quantum alliance as some 6 million BTC sit in exposed addresses, and Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has proposed "quantum landmines" to make attacks on such coins costly.

Layer-2 networks are not insulated either. Optimistic rollups could face forged signatures during their dispute windows, typically seven days on Ethereum, and many zero-knowledge rollups use SNARK proofs that rely on elliptic curves. Hash-based STARK proofs are more resistant, but a rollup is only as safe as the layer-1 contracts, bridges and governance keys it depends on, the report mentioned.

Developers are already working on fixes. Researchers have proposed several ways to make Bitcoin quantum-safe, StarkWare has shown a quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction, and Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has said the network is betting its future on quantum resistance.

IOSCO said firms should migrate to post-quantum cryptography and build "crypto-agility," the ability to update cryptographic systems without major redesign. Quantum key distribution could complement those measures on selected high-security channels, it added.

Most preparations across financial markets are still at an early stage, focused on awareness, governance, training and identifying vulnerable systems, according to the report, which drew on a March 2026 survey of members of IOSCO's Fintech Task Force and discussions with experts. Some respondents described "quantum-procrastination," in which firms put off action while waiting for clearer regulatory signals or wider adoption.

No surveyed jurisdiction reported operational deployment of quantum computing in regulated financial services. The watchdog also urged regulators to act against "quantum washing," in which firms overstate the role, maturity or performance of quantum technology. IOSCO said it will treat quantum as a priority in 2027, focusing on raising awareness across the financial ecosystem.

Quantum hardware is advancing quickly. IBM has claimed a trusted quantum advantage, and Google has mentioned it has cracked some of the field's biggest bottlenecks.
